issues.legal_issue: A statutory town-planning scheme does not violate equality or property guarantees merely because land vests through the scheme and compensation is determined under a distinct procedure rather than the general land-acquisition procedure.
material_facts: The challenged scheme formed part of an urban development plan involving allocation and reconstitution of land, rather than an isolated acquisition of land for a single public purpose.
When the final scheme took effect, land required by the local authority vested in it by operation of law.
The scheme provided for reconstituted plots and financial adjustments, including compensation based on the market value of the original and reconstituted plots at the prescribed point.
The land-acquisition procedure and its appeal mechanisms were not applied to vesting under the town-planning scheme.
issues.conclusion: The distinct town-planning procedure and compensation mechanism did not make the scheme unconstitutional or discriminatory under Articles 14 or 31 of the Constitution.
issues.legal_principle: The Bombay Town Planning Act, 1954 must be considered as an integrated urban-planning scheme, not as a series of isolated acquisitions. Sections 53, 66, 67, 71 and 73 provide for vesting, contributions, compensation and financial adjustments; the market value of land remains relevant. The distinct procedure is not discriminatory merely because the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, including its procedures under sections 18 and 54, does not apply. The Court applied State of Gujarat v. Shri Shantilal Mangaldas, Maneklal Chhotalal v. M.G. Makwana and The Zandu Pharmaceutical Works Ltd. v. G.J. Desai.

rule.if: town_planning_scheme_challenge and integrated_urban_plan and statutory_reconstitution_and_adjustment and market_value_remains_relevant

predicates.town_planning_scheme_challenge: The proceeding challenges the constitutionality of a statutory town-planning scheme.
predicates.integrated_urban_plan: The local authority uses the scheme as part of an integrated plan for orderly urban development.
predicates.statutory_reconstitution_and_adjustment: The scheme provides for reconstituted plots or financial adjustments when land is taken or rights are altered.
predicates.market_value_remains_relevant: The compensation or adjustment mechanism takes the market value of the affected land into account.

issues.definition: When a town-planning challenge concerns an integrated urban plan with statutory reconstitution or adjustment and market value remains relevant, the distinct scheme procedure is not unconstitutional on that ground.

issues.legal_issue: The absence of an appeal against some decisions made by an officer under a statute does not, by itself, make the statutory procedure discriminatory or arbitrary.
material_facts: The statute provided appeals to a board for some categories of decisions by the town planning officer but not for the compensation determination at issue.
The town planning officer exercised defined functions as part of implementing the scheme.
A person aggrieved by an order could seek relief under Article 226 of the Constitution.
issues.conclusion: The lack of an appeal against the compensation determination did not make the statutory procedure unconstitutional or confer uncanalised and arbitrary power on the officer.
issues.legal_principle: There is no general rule that every decision of every statutory officer must be appealable. A lack of appeal warrants constitutional condemnation only where it is likely to make the procedure oppressive and arbitrary. The Court relied on M/s Babubhai & Co. v. State of Gujarat and noted the availability of relief under Article 226.

rule.if: statutory_officer_decision_challenge and appeal_exists_for_some_decisions_but_not_this_one and officer_has_defined_functions and judicial_review_remains_available

predicates.statutory_officer_decision_challenge: The proceeding challenges a statutory process because a decision by an officer cannot be appealed.
predicates.appeal_exists_for_some_decisions_but_not: The statute allows appeals against some decisions by the officer but not against the decision at issue.
predicates.officer_has_defined_functions: The officer performs functions defined by the statutory scheme rather than exercising unbounded authority.
predicates.judicial_review_remains_available: An aggrieved person may seek judicial review of the officer's decision.

issues.definition: Where a challenge concerns an unappealable statutory decision, the officer has defined functions and judicial review remains available, the absence of an appeal alone does not make the procedure unconstitutional.

issues.legal_issue: The absence of a solatium under a town-planning scheme does not, by itself, make its compensation mechanism discriminatory.
material_facts: The challenged scheme provided compensation and financial adjustments under its own integrated planning mechanism but did not provide the solatium available under the Land Acquisition Act.
The scheme involved automatic vesting upon the final scheme taking effect, possible allotment of reconstituted plots, and financial adjustments between landowners and the local authority.
It was not shown that the compensation payable was illusory or unreal.
issues.conclusion: The absence of solatium did not make the town-planning scheme discriminatory, and the compensation mechanism was not shown to be illusory or unreal.
issues.legal_principle: A town-planning scheme that operates through automatic vesting, reconstituted plots and financial adjustments is not equivalent to a conventional acquisition under the Land Acquisition Act. The absence of solatium does not alone establish discrimination, and the public interest in providing and maintaining public services is also relevant. The Court distinguished Nagpur Improvement Trust v. Vithal Rao, State of Kerala v. T.N. Peter and P.C. Goswami v. Collector of Darrang.

rule.if: town_planning_scheme_challenge and automatic_vesting_with_reconstitution and no_solarium_provided and compensation_not_shown_illusory

predicates.town_planning_scheme_challenge: The proceeding challenges the constitutionality of a statutory town-planning scheme.
predicates.automatic_vesting_with_reconstitution: The scheme provides for land to vest by operation of law and allows for reconstituted plots or related financial adjustments.
predicates.no_solarium_provided: The scheme does not provide an additional payment of the kind sometimes awarded alongside compensation.
predicates.compensation_not_shown_illusory: The challenger has not shown that the compensation payable is unreal or illusory.

issues.definition: If a town-planning scheme provides for automatic vesting with reconstitution, does not provide an additional payment, and its compensation is not shown to be illusory, the absence of that payment does not make the scheme discriminatory.

issues.legal_issue: A precedent upholding a statute remains binding unless it is overruled, and later decisions do not overrule it merely by describing it as virtually or substantially overruled.
material_facts: A Constitution Bench had previously upheld the town-planning statute.
Later decisions contained observations characterising that earlier decision as virtually or substantially overruled, but did not expressly overrule it.
A later decision had quoted and relied on the earlier decision, and no subsequent decision had struck down the statute.
issues.conclusion: The earlier Constitution Bench decision remained binding and had not been overruled by the later decisions relied on by the challenger.
issues.legal_principle: A precedent binds through the principle underlying its decision, which must be identified in light of the case in which it was decided; its scope should not be enlarged beyond that context. A Constitution Bench considering the effect of a precedent must examine it and form its own view rather than rely on imprecise descriptions in later decisions. The Court considered R.C. Cooper v. Union of India, Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala and State of Karnataka v. Ranganatha Reddy, and referred to Temperton v. Russell, Allen v. Flood and Quinn v. Leathem.

rule.if: court_considers_precedent_effect and earlier_constitution_bench_upheld_law and no_later_express_overruling and later_decisions_only_described_precedent_as_overruled

predicates.court_considers_precedent_effect: The proceeding requires the court to determine whether an earlier precedent remains authoritative.
predicates.earlier_constitution_bench_upheld_law: An earlier Constitution Bench upheld the law at issue.
predicates.no_later_express_overruling: No later decision expressly overruled the earlier precedent.
predicates.later_decisions_only_described_precedent: Later decisions used imprecise descriptions of the earlier precedent's status without expressly overruling it.

issues.definition: When a court considers precedent effect, an earlier Constitution Bench upheld the law, no later decision expressly overruled it, and later decisions only described it as overruled, the earlier precedent remains binding.
